desc:
A faulty keyboard sometimes presses the Home and End keys by itself. The string keys lists the key presses in order: a lowercase letter types that letter at the current cursor position, the character '[' is Home (the cursor jumps to the very beginning of the text), and ']' is End (the cursor jumps to the very end of the text). The text starts empty with the cursor at the end.

Return the final text. It may be empty if no letters were typed.

Example: 'ab[cd]ef' gives 'cdabef': cd is typed at the front, then End moves back to the end for ef. Another: '[a[b]c' gives 'bac'.
constraints: keys consists of lowercase letters, '[' and ']'
The answer may be the empty string
hints: Inserting into the middle of a Python string or list for every letter makes the simulation O(n<sup>2</sup>) in the worst case.
Between two special keys the typed letters form one block that stays together. Where does a whole block end up?

Collect each block. If the key before it was Home, the block goes to the very front (before all earlier front blocks); otherwise it goes to the very end. Keep front blocks in a stack or deque and join everything at the end.
editorial: Split the key presses into maximal runs of letters separated by [ and ]. All letters of a run are typed one after another at the same place, and a run typed after Home is placed at the very front of the text, in front of everything typed earlier, including earlier front runs. A run typed in End mode (the starting mode too) is appended after everything.

So keep two lists: front receives each Home run in order of typing and is reversed at the end, and back receives each End run in order. The answer is the reversed front joined with back. This avoids any middle insertion and is O(n) time and space.
